extracted.intended_audience: playwrights, dramatists, actors, theatre-producers, and critics (readers interested in dramatic composition and stagecraft)
extracted.subtask_description: Advice and prescriptive criteria for composing and staging tragic plays, with emphasis on what to represent onstage versus what to narrate, how to move pity and terror, and how stage dress and effects should support (not substitute for) the writing. Draws on examples from English, French, and ancient drama.

rubrics_metrics.name: Raise terror and pity by sentiments and expression, not stage dress
rubrics_metrics.description: Ordinary writers in tragedy attempt to raise terror and pity not by proper sentiments and expressions but by the dresses and decorations of the stage (per Aristotle). The imagination should be moved by the dignity of thought and sublimity of expression rather than external trappings.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recommend composing language and ideas that inspire grand conceptions (e.g., Shakespeare's Brutus) instead of relying on robes, plumes, or other ornaments. Example guidance: 'I would have our Conceptions raised by the Dignity of Thought and Sublimity of Expression, rather than by a Train of Robes or a Plume of Feathers.' Anti-pattern: making the audience feel grandeur because of a big hat or robe rather than the words.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid extravagant head-ornaments and sweeping trains that distract
rubrics_metrics.description: Huge plumes on heads and broad sweeping trains are used to make a person appear great, but they force actors into stiff, self-conscious behavior and divert the audience's attention to the costume or the attendant who manages it.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not let costume trappings dictate the actor's posture or the audience's focus. Specific anti-patterns: an actor holding his neck stiff to preserve a plume, or attention fixed on a page opening a queen's train instead of her speech. Solution: simplify costume so acting and speech can convey dignity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not present large armies or battles literally onstage—narrate them
rubrics_metrics.description: Small numbers of actors with halberts and a few porters cannot credibly represent armies or huge battles; such representation strains imagination and looks absurd.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Tellers/readers can generate more vivid ideas of a battle through description than a cramped stage can by spectacle. Recommendation: relate or describe battles and mass events rather than attempting to stage them literally; follow the French practice of leaving guards behind the scenes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use mechanical/visual effects (thunder, lightning, ghosts) sparingly and with skill
rubrics_metrics.description: Thunder, lightning, bells, and ghost entrances can be effective in creating terror or attention when introduced with skill and accompanied by appropriate sentiments and preceding discourse.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When used well they enhance effect (examples: the clock in Venice Preserved, the Ghost in Hamlet). But they must be integrated into the writing—don't rely on them as a substitute for proper dramatic sentiment. Avoid gratuitous or excessive use purely to shock.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid noisy pageantry (drums, trumpets, huzzas) that overwhelms the play
rubrics_metrics.description: The noise of drums, trumpets, and huzzas (and other loud pageant effects) can be excessive and drown the drama or appear vulgar, especially when used to represent battles or grandeur.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prefer restraint; leave noisy martial celebrations offstage or curtail their use so as not to overpower speech and sentiment. The French stage's restraint is offered as a model.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ensure physical displays of grief (handkerchiefs, tears) are matched by the actor's speech
rubrics_metrics.description: In common tragedies the handkerchief is a primary instrument for showing sorrow, but it should not be misapplied; the actor's tongue must 'sympathize with his eyes.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use such props judiciously and ensure that the dialogue and performance justify and amplify physical signs of sorrow; avoid mechanical, unmotivated displays that feel contrived.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not multiply child-victims or contrived familial scenes purely to manufacture pity
rubrics_metrics.description: Introducing one child can draw compassion; however, doubling or tripling children purely to outdo predecessors becomes ridiculous when handled badly.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid escalating the number of children or other sentimental devices as a cheap method to 'break hearts.' Pity must arise naturally from credible circumstances and sincere writing, not contrivance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid on-stage depictions of murder, torture, and excessive bloodshed—prefer off-stage execution and reported speech
rubrics_metrics.description: Graphic representations of stabbing, poisoning, racking, impaling, and scenes crowded with carcasses are brutal, barbarous, and invite ridicule. Such acts often look indecent and cruel when shown literally.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prefer to have violent acts occur off-stage and be recounted or heard as cries/dialogue (example: Sophocles' handling of Orestes; the mother-son dialogue carried out behind the scenes). This preserves decency and can be more affecting than explicit onstage violence. The French practice of transacting murders behind the scenes is cited as a preferable model.

rubrics_metrics.name: Certain incidents are improper for direct representation onstage—tell rather than show
rubrics_metrics.description: There are things 'improper for a scene' that men of judgment will relate instead of representing directly (Horace quoted). Some dramatic incidents, by their nature, work better when narrated than acted out.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess which events the stage can convincingly and tastefully show; move others into narrative, reported dialogue, or off-stage action. This overlaps with advice about battles and murders but applies more broadly to any scene that cannot be satisfactorily staged.

rubrics_metrics.name: Beware spectacle (tailor and painter) substituting for good writing—vulgar audiences are taken in by show
rubrics_metrics.description: Tailors and painters (costume and set) often contribute more to a play's success with ordinary audiences than the poet; scenes and appearances can trick ordinary minds as much as speeches.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not let spectacle compensate for weak writing. Understand that spectacle may bring an audience but discerning viewers will 'see through' mere appearances. The Italian term 'Fourberia della Scena' (the knavery or trickish part of the drama) is cited as the practice of imposing on spectators by appearances.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prefer natural facial expression and animated features over cosmetic artifice in characters' appearance
rubrics_metrics.description: Painted faces and make-up that create fixed, lifeless complexions (the 'Picts') simulate beauty but lack animated, responsive features; genuine faces ('British') show soft passion, surprise, and agreeable confusion.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid admitting characters (especially women) who conceal their natural visage with artifice and expect intimacy; such artifice undermines believable expression and can offend on close approach. The essay recommends valuing natural looks that reflect feeling; anecdote: Honeycomb's lover discovered to be painted, curing his infatuation.
